Categorical distal outcome by class (Mplus DCAT)

dcat.Rd

Probabilities of a categorical distal outcome in each latent class by the method of Lanza, Tan & Bray (2013), as Mplus AUXILIARY = y (DCAT), with Wald tests of equal distributions across classes.

Usage

dcat(object, data, y, ref = NULL, name = NULL)

Arguments

object

A fitted latentmix model without covariates (K >= 2).

data

Data frame with one row per row of the data the model was fitted to, or (backward compatible) the numeric outcome vector itself with y omitted.

y

Outcome column of data (tidyselect, one column): factor, character, logical or numeric category codes. Factor-like labels are kept for output.

ref

Reference class for the odds ratios (default: the last class).

name

Label of the outcome in output (default: the column name, else "y").

Value

An object of class c("latentmix_dcat", "latentmix_aux"), a list with name, probs, se and oddsratio (class-by-category matrices), ref, levels, overall (overall Wald test: chisq, df, p), pairwise (data frame of pairwise tests), n, ndeleted and text.

Details

The latent class is regressed on indicators of the outcome categories jointly with the measurement model (started from object), and \(P(y \mid \mathrm{class})\) follows by Bayes' theorem. Standard errors are obtained by the delta method from the robust covariance matrix. Odds ratios compare each category with the first, relative to class ref. Rows with a missing outcome are deleted. data must have one row per row of the data the model was fitted to, in the same order. With a complex survey design in object (cluster, strata) the standard errors are design-based; Mplus does not offer DCAT with TYPE = MIXTURE COMPLEX, so this case has no Mplus counterpart.

References

Lanza, S. T., Tan, X., & Bray, B. C. (2013). Latent class analysis with distal outcomes: A flexible model-based approach. Structural Equation Modeling, 20(1), 1–26. doi:10.1080/10705511.2013.742377

Asparouhov, T., & Muthén, B. (2014). Auxiliary variables in mixture modeling: Three-step approaches using Mplus. Structural Equation Modeling, 21(3), 329–341. doi:10.1080/10705511.2014.915181

See also

bch(), r3step(), lm_table().

Examples

data(aces)
# \donttest{
# Self-rated health (srh: 1 excellent ... 5 poor) across the ACE classes
m <- lca(aces, starts_with("ace_"), K = 4)     # 4 ACE classes, as generated
#> Starting Julia ...
d <- dcat(m, aces, srh, ref = 1)
d$probs       # P(srh category | class): fair/poor health is most common with high adversity
#>                 1         2         3          4          5
#> class1 0.24514728 0.3950810 0.2544518 0.07933881 0.02598117
#> class2 0.17096747 0.2935717 0.3143047 0.14677180 0.07438429
#> class3 0.16395870 0.3460778 0.3015224 0.16422576 0.02421531
#> class4 0.09266795 0.2879063 0.3192313 0.23986835 0.06032609
d$oddsratio   # odds ratios against class 1 (Low adversity)
#>        1        2        3        4        5
#> class1 1 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000
#> class2 1 1.065471 1.771165 2.652593 4.105217
#> class3 1 1.309725 1.771768 3.094911 1.393554
#> class4 1 1.927803 3.318925 7.998063 6.142484
# }
